/services/cyber-security-for-ot-and-ics.intro: Operational technology is not office IT. Controls, power, and safety systems cannot simply be patched or rebooted on a schedule. We help you understand what is connected, close the most important gaps first, and do it in a way that respects uptime and the people who depend on it.

cards.title: Know what is connected
cards.copy: We build a clear picture of devices, networks, and remote access paths, including the ones added years ago and never written down.

cards.title: Fix the right things first

process.title: Strengthen
process.copy: Support segmentation, access controls, and documentation, and leave your team with a plan they can maintain.

outcomes: A current, shared view of connected systems
Fewer unmanaged paths into critical equipment
A practical roadmap tied to operations

problems.title: Systems nobody has inventoried
problems.copy: If you cannot list what is on the network, you cannot protect it. A good inventory is the foundation for everything that follows.

problems.title: Open remote access
problems.copy: Vendor connections and shared credentials are among the most common weak points. We review who can reach what, from where, and why.

problems.title: Flat networks
problems.copy: When building systems share a network with everything else, a problem in one place can spread. Segmentation guidance reduces that risk without disrupting operations.

problems.title: Legacy equipment that cannot be patched
problems.copy: Older controllers are normal in real facilities. We recommend compensating measures that fit equipment you cannot simply replace.

faqs.question: What does RJY Group do, and which facilities do you serve?
faqs.answer: RJY Group is a Houston-based facilities and infrastructure partner. We support building automation, operational technology (OT) and industrial control system (ICS) cybersecurity, HVAC and chiller plants, standby generators, water treatment, and technical staffing. Our clients include hospitals, government and public safety facilities, industrial and commercial campuses, universities, data centers, and transportation and utility operators.

faqs.question: Is RJY Group a certified small business, and how can I verify it?
faqs.answer: Yes. RJY Group is a Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Business (SDVOSB) verified through the VA's Center for Verification and Evaluation (CVE), an SBA 8(a) certified firm, and a GSA Schedule holder (contract 47QSMS25D008U). We are also recognized by the City of Houston and VetHUB. Certification details and links to the official registries are on our Certifications page.

faqs.question: How can a government agency or public entity procure services from RJY Group?
faqs.answer: Agencies can buy through our GSA Schedule contract, or use SDVOSB and 8(a) set-aside and sole-source authorities where they apply to the acquisition. Applicability depends on the contract value, scope, and your agency's rules, so we recommend confirming the route with your contracting officer. We will gladly supply capability statements, pricing, and past-performance references to support the file.

faqs.question: Where do you work, and can you support multiple sites?
faqs.answer: Our headquarters is in Houston, Texas, and we support facilities across the Gulf Coast, Texas, and the wider region. Many clients have several buildings or campuses, and we can standardize service, reporting, and response across all of them under one agreement. If your sites are outside our usual area, contact us and we will tell you plainly what we can support.

faqs.question: How quickly can you respond to an urgent system failure?
faqs.answer: We maintain 24/7 critical response for the systems we support. For a live outage, call the Houston office directly rather than using the website form, because a phone call reaches a specialist fastest. Actual arrival time depends on your location and the nature of the failure, so we define response targets in writing in your service agreement instead of promising a number in advance.

faqs.question: What happens during a first assessment or site inspection?
faqs.answer: We walk the facility with your team, review the systems in scope, and ask how the building actually operates, including any past failures. We then document asset condition, risks, and gaps, and rank them by consequence and urgency. You receive a written summary with recommended next steps, so you can decide what to fund and when, with no obligation to proceed.

faqs.question: How is pricing structured, and can I get a fixed quote?
faqs.answer: It depends on the work. Defined projects such as a controls upgrade or a generator overhaul are normally quoted as a fixed price against a written scope. Ongoing maintenance is priced as a recurring agreement, and urgent or open-ended repairs may be time and materials with a not-to-exceed limit. Every option is itemized in advance, so you are never surprised by an invoice.

faqs.question: Do you offer planned maintenance agreements, or only call-out repairs?
faqs.answer: Both. Most of our long-term clients choose planned maintenance because it reduces emergency calls and extends equipment life. Agreements set inspection schedules, testing, reporting, and response terms for each system. If you only need a repair, a one-time project, or a second opinion on a failing asset, we can do that as well, and many relationships grow from there.

faqs.question: What does your building automation work cover?
faqs.answer: We assess, optimize, integrate, and maintain building automation systems (BAS). Typical work includes reviewing control sequences, correcting overrides and failed sensors, tuning schedules for comfort and energy, improving alarms and trending, integrating separate systems into one operating view, and planning phased upgrades. The aim is a building that runs predictably and gives your team data they can trust.

faqs.question: Do we have to replace our existing controls or equipment to work with you?
faqs.answer: No. We work with existing control platforms and major equipment manufacturers, and we start by improving what you already own. Replacement is recommended only when an asset is unsupported, unsafe, or no longer cost effective to keep, and we show the evidence behind that advice. Phased upgrades let you spread capital cost over several budget cycles.

faqs.question: What does OT and ICS cybersecurity support include, and will it disrupt operations?
faqs.answer: We start by identifying the connected building and industrial systems you actually have, then assess network segmentation, remote access, passwords, patching, and monitoring against recognized frameworks such as NIST SP 800-82 and IEC 62443. Discovery is done carefully, favoring passive methods, and any change is scheduled with your operations team so that critical systems are not put at risk.

faqs.question: How do you keep HVAC and chiller plants reliable?
faqs.answer: We combine scheduled preventive maintenance with performance trending, so problems show up in the data before they become outages. Work covers chillers, boilers, air handlers, pumps, cooling towers, and controls, with seasonal readiness checks ahead of peak load. Refrigerant handling follows EPA requirements, and every visit ends with a report on condition and recommended repairs.

faqs.question: How do you support facilities that cannot afford downtime, such as hospitals and data centers?
faqs.answer: We plan before we touch anything. That means written method statements, agreed maintenance windows, awareness of redundancy and failover paths, and coordination with your operations, infection control, and life-safety teams. Work is phased so that backup capacity stays available, and we confirm systems are back to normal before we leave the site.

faqs.question: What is included in generator service, and do you provide compliance records?
faqs.answer: Our generator program covers inspections, fluid and filter service, battery and starting system checks, fuel quality testing, automatic transfer switch testing, and load bank testing. We keep records aligned with NFPA 110 and with your accreditation needs, so you have organized, audit-ready documentation showing the equipment will perform when the utility fails.

faqs.question: How does water treatment protect our equipment and our occupants?
faqs.answer: Chemistry in closed-loop and cooling tower systems directly affects scale, corrosion, energy use, and biological risk. We test the water, adjust treatment programs, and keep logs, so chillers, boilers, and heat exchangers last longer and run efficiently. Where needed, we support Legionella risk management plans consistent with ASHRAE Standard 188.

faqs.question: How does your support staffing work?
faqs.answer: We provide qualified technical personnel, such as building engineers, controls technicians, operators, and maintenance specialists, to extend your facilities team. You can use them for temporary coverage, project surges, or long-term placements. We screen credentials and experience, and can meet your background check and site-access requirements before anyone arrives.

faqs.question: What safety, insurance, and site-access requirements do you meet?
faqs.answer: Safety comes first on every job. Our people follow written safety procedures, complete your site-specific orientation, and wear appropriate protective equipment. We can provide certificates of insurance and safety documentation on request, and we comply with background checks, badging, escort, and security rules, including those at government and healthcare facilities.

faqs.question: What documentation and reporting will we receive?
faqs.answer: After each visit you receive a clear service report covering what was inspected, what was done, what was found, and what we recommend, with deficiencies ranked by priority. Asset condition, test results, and corrective actions are kept in an organized record, so your team can plan budgets, answer auditors, and see trends over time.

faqs.question: How do you make sure the work meets code, standards, and audit expectations?
faqs.answer: We identify the codes and standards that apply to each system, such as NFPA, ASHRAE, OSHA, and healthcare accreditation requirements, and build inspection and test routines around them. Results are documented in the form inspectors and auditors expect. We tell you plainly if something falls short and what it takes to correct it.

faqs.question: How do you limit disruption to occupants and daily operations?
faqs.answer: We schedule work around your operating calendar, using after-hours or phased approaches when needed. Occupants and department leads are notified in advance, work areas are controlled and cleaned, and systems are never taken offline without an agreed plan. A single point of contact keeps everyone informed from start to finish.

It helps to have a list of the systems involved, recent issues, and any deadlines or compliance drivers. For a life-safety emergency, follow your own emergency procedure first, then call us.

sections: When the team keeps manual overrides, sticky notes, and personal tricks to keep a building comfortable, the system is no longer doing its job. Workarounds hide the real problem and keep knowledge in people’s heads instead of in the system.

If operators silence alarms out of habit, a real event can slip past. A healthy alarm list is short, ranked, and trusted. Reviewing alarm history and resetting priorities is often the quickest win available.

Buildings change. Rooms are repurposed, equipment is replaced, and schedules shift. If the screens and sequences still describe the building as it was years ago, decisions will rest on bad information.
When a complaint comes in and nobody can tell what the system was doing at the time, troubleshooting becomes guesswork. Trending the right points gives you evidence rather than opinions.
Edits made in a hurry and never recorded add up. Consistent change records make the next fix faster and the next audit easier.

sections: Start by listing the devices and networks that make up your building and industrial systems, and how they connect. Even a rough inventory reveals surprises and gives every later decision something solid to stand on.
Every system needs a named owner on your side and a clear picture of which vendors support it. When something goes wrong, nobody should be asking who is responsible.
Vendor connections, shared accounts, and forgotten remote tools are common weak points. Find out who can connect, from where, and with what credentials, then tighten whatever is not needed.
Not every finding is equally pressing. Fix the few things that put critical operations at real risk first, and place the rest on a sensible roadmap.
Security changes in OT environments can affect running equipment. Plan them with the people who operate the building so safety and availability stay protected.

faqs.answer: Early enough to leave time for parts, repairs, and testing, which usually means well before the first hot or cold stretch.

sections: Start with what went wrong last time. Open work orders, recurring alarms, and complaints from the last peak are the best predictors of what will fail next.
Check that scheduled maintenance and tests have actually been completed and recorded. Gaps are far easier to close in spring than in the middle of a heat wave.
Make sure sensors read correctly, sequences are in the right seasonal mode, and alarms will reach the right people.
Know which parts have long lead times and have them on hand or identified. Keep current contact details for the people you will need to call.
Decide beforehand who makes the call when something fails, who is notified, and what happens next. A short, shared plan saves time under pressure.
